items.a: Strong **CS fundamentals** (programming, system design, algorithms) **plus fluent agentic workflows** — not vibe-coding alone. A single developer increasingly becomes a **manager of agents**.

items.q: Why is multi-agent orchestration the "last boss"?
items.a: Handling multiple agents well puts you in the **top ~0.1% of users today**. More agents does **not** mean better systems — undirected sprawl can make things worse.

items.q: Should you run 10 agents on day one like Boris?
items.a: No — that's the **wrong outcome to emphasize**. Master **one agent workflow**, then add isolated tasks (logo fix, header copy) **one agent at a time**.

items.q: What human-management skill transfers to agents?
items.a: **Context switching**. Agents are eager interns — you watch terminals and jump between stuck tasks, the same skill as managing human developers with **isolated task boundaries**.

items.q: What do agents need to operate safely?
items.a: Agents operate on **explicitly defined contracts**. **Tests = contracts** agents can verify; no tests = no contracts. Stale READMEs and inconsistent design patterns confuse agents the way they confuse humans.

items.q: Why do agent errors get so bad so fast?
items.a: **Error compounding**: one misunderstanding in step 1 gets **doubled down in step 2**. The foundation must be airtight before you delegate.

items.q: Why is the junior market so brutal right now?
items.a: Three forces: post-COVID **over-hiring then layoffs**, CS grads **~2–3×** since Eric's cohort, and employers preferring fewer **AI-native** hires. Anecdote: Berkeley grad, **~1,000 apps → ~2 replies**.
